title: Ezekiel 33:21–33
context: A date is given: “In the twelfth year of our captivity, in the tenth month, in the fifth day of the month,” one who had escaped from Jerusalem comes to the prophet with the news, “The city has been defeated!” (33:21). How this date lines up with the account of the city’s fall in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 depends on how the years are reckoned, and readers calculate the interval differently. The evening before, the LORD’s hand was on the prophet, and his mouth was opened, so that he was “no longer mute” (33:22). This ties back to 3:26–27 and fulfills 24:25–27. The LORD then answers the claim of those living in the ruins of the land: “Abraham was one, and he inherited the land; but we are many” (33:24). He lists their sins and announces that the land will become “a desolation and an astonishment” (33:25–29). Finally the LORD tells the prophet that the exiles talk about him and come to hear him, but “they hear your words, but don’t do them”; to them he is like “a very lovely song” (33:30–32). When the word comes to pass, “they will know that a prophet has been among them” (33:33). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the fall of the city vindicates the prophet’s word, and hearing must lead to doing.

verses.text: In the twelfth year of our captivity, in the tenth month, in the fifth day of the month, one who had escaped out of Jerusalem came to me, saying, “The city has been defeated!”
verses.arminianNotes: A survivor “who had escaped out of Jerusalem” arrives with the news, “The city has been defeated!” Arminian readers note that the word the prophet had long announced has now come to pass. The date is given precisely, though readers reckon its relation to the city’s fall in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s word vindicated in history, as the prophet’s warnings are confirmed by the event. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the exact calendar reckoning and read the verse as the hinge of the book, turning from judgment toward the promises of restoration that follow.

verses.text: Now the LORD’s hand had been on me in the evening, before he who had escaped came; and he had opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning; and my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s hand was on the prophet “in the evening,” and “my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute.” Arminian readers note that the silence announced in 3:26–27 ends just as 24:25–27 said it would. The prophet now speaks freely to a people who have seen the word fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD both closing and opening the prophet’s mouth according to his word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse in its literary context, tying it back to 3:26–27 and 24:25–27, and see it as a sign that the LORD’s timing governs his messenger’s speech.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came to me, saying”. Arminian readers note that the first word after the opening of the prophet’s mouth is addressed to a new situation: those left in the ruined land. The prophet’s renewed speech is again the LORD’s own message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD directing his prophet’s freshly opened mouth to the next task. Shared ground: both traditions read the formula as marking a new oracle, and as showing that the prophet’s speech after his silence remains under the LORD’s command.

verses.text: “Son of man, those who inhabit the waste places in the land of Israel speak, saying, ‘Abraham was one, and he inherited the land; but we are many. The land is given us for inheritance.’
verses.arminianNotes: Those in “the waste places in the land of Israel” say, “Abraham was one, and he inherited the land; but we are many. The land is given us for inheritance.” Arminian readers note the false confidence of claiming a promise while ignoring the faith and obedience that went with it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a presumptuous appeal to the promise made to Abraham, used as a guarantee apart from covenant faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as warning against resting on descent or numbers, a theme that echoes in John 8:39 and Matthew 3:9, each in its own setting.

verses.text: Therefore tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “You eat with the blood, and lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood. So should you possess the land?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers, “You eat with the blood, and lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood. So should you possess the land?” Arminian readers note that the claim to the promise is exposed by the people’s conduct. Their way of life contradicts the inheritance they boast in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD measuring the claim against his law, naming food laws, idolatry, and bloodshed. Shared ground: both traditions read the question “So should you possess the land?” as a rhetorical rebuke, showing that the land was never held apart from faithfulness to the LORD.

verses.text: You stand on your sword, you work abomination, and every one of you defiles his neighbor’s wife. So should you possess the land?” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “You stand on your sword, you work abomination,” and they wrong their neighbors’ marriages. Arminian readers note that violence and broken faith with one another are listed alongside idolatry. The repeated question “So should you possess the land?” drives the point home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see sins against God and neighbor joined together, as in the law itself. Shared ground: both traditions read the charges soberly and without elaboration, and both hear the repeated question as the LORD’s verdict on a claim made without repentance.

verses.text: “You shall tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “As I live, surely those who are in the waste places will fall by the sword. I will give whoever is in the open field to the animals to be devoured, and those who are in the strongholds and in the caves will die of the pestilence.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD swears, “As I live,” that those in the waste places, the open field, and the strongholds will fall to sword, animals, and pestilence. Arminian readers note that the same oath that declared “no pleasure” in 33:11 now confirms judgment on those who refuse to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s oath binding him to his word in judgment as in mercy. Shared ground: both traditions read the familiar threefold judgment soberly, as covenant curse falling on those who claimed the land while despising the LORD, and neither dwells on the violence.

verses.text: I will make the land a desolation and an astonishment. The pride of her power will cease. The mountains of Israel will be desolate, so that no one will pass through.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make the land a desolation and an astonishment. The pride of her power will cease.” Arminian readers note that the land itself bears the marks of judgment, and that the pride the people trusted in is brought low.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD humbling the pride of the land so that no one will pass through. Shared ground: both traditions read the desolation as the reversal of the claim in 33:24, and both see in it the seriousness of presuming on God’s gifts.

verses.text: Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolation and an astonishment because of all their abominations which they have committed.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the purpose of judgment is that the LORD be known, and that the desolation comes “because of all their abominations which they have committed.” The cause lies in the people’s own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD making himself known through his righteous acts, with the people’s abominations as the stated cause. Shared ground: both traditions read the recognition formula, common in Ezekiel, as the goal of the LORD’s dealings in judgment and in restoration.

verses.text: “As for you, son of man, the children of your people talk about you by the walls and in the doors of the houses, and speak to one another, everyone to his brother, saying, ‘Please come and hear what the word is that comes out from the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes: The exiles “talk about you by the walls and in the doors of the houses,” saying, “Please come and hear what the word is that comes out from the LORD.” Arminian readers note the irony: the prophet has become a popular topic, yet interest is not the same as obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a people who treat the LORD’s word as something to discuss rather than to obey. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the problem of 33:31–32, that the prophet is now heard eagerly but not heeded.

verses.text: They come to you as the people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain.
verses.arminianNotes: “they hear your words, but don’t do them; for with their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after their gain.” Arminian readers note the gap between profession and obedience, and see the call to respond as real. Compare James 1:22 in passing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a divided heart, with outward devotion masking a heart set on gain. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that hearing without doing deceives the hearer, and both note the kinship with James 1:22 without making the two passages say the same thing.

verses.text: Behold, you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument; for they hear your words, but they don’t do them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet, “you are to them as a very lovely song of one who has a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument”. Arminian readers note that the people enjoy the prophet as entertainment. The repeated charge, “they hear your words, but they don’t do them”, is the heart of the verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a congregation that admires the messenger while ignoring the message. Shared ground: both traditions read the image of the love song as a searching word to every hearer of preaching, who may enjoy the sound of the word without being changed by it.

verses.text: “When this comes to pass—behold, it comes—then they will know that a prophet has been among them.”
verses.arminianNotes: “When this comes to pass” then “they will know that a prophet has been among them.” Arminian readers note that the fulfillment of the word will vindicate the prophet, and that the hearers are still accountable for how they listened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD vindicating his messenger by bringing his word to pass. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse as echoing 2:5, where the LORD told the prophet that whether the people hear or refuse, “yet they will know that there has been a prophet among them.”
